title: Propositions and Logical Expressions
summary: This unit introduces discrete mathematics (Diskrete Mathematik), unambiguity, and expressions in propositional logic. You will learn about logical connectives (Junktoren), quantifiers (Quantoren), truth tables (Wahrheitstabellen), and logical equivalence (logische Gleichwertigkeit). You will also determine solution sets of propositional forms and use counterexamples.
keyFacts: Discrete mathematics studies distinguishable objects, sets, systems, and structures.
The objects in a countable set can be numbered using natural numbers.
Parentheses and punctuation help structure expressions unambiguously; parenthesized expressions belong to the Dyck language.
A definition establishes the meaning of a term in a particular context.
A proposition is the content of a declarative sentence.
Logical connectives combine propositions; “not” is unary.
The quantifiers $\forall$, $\exists$, and $\nexists$ stand for “for all,” “there exists,” and “there exists no,” respectively.
In a syllogism, “All A are B” and “All B are C” imply “All A are C.”
A truth table covers all assignments of $A$ and $B$; $w$ means true and $f$ means false.
And, or, if and only if, and exclusive or are symmetric; implication is asymmetric.
Substituting a value into a propositional form yields a proposition; its solution set contains all values for which it is true.
A single counterexample is enough to refute the general validity of a claim.

questions.prompt: Which description applies to discrete mathematics?

options.text: It deals only with real numbers.
It studies distinguishable objects, sets, systems, and structures.
It studies only continuous quantities with no individual elements.
It describes space and time exclusively using models without gaps.

questions.explanation: Discrete mathematics studies individual, distinguishable objects and structures. Continuous models without gaps are a contrast to the discrete; they are not part of its definition.

questions.prompt: Which sets are classified as countable? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, and $\mathbb{Q}$ are countable. The lecture notes classify $\mathbb{R}$ as uncountable.

questions.prompt: A continuous structure consists of individual, distinguishable elements with no gaps.
questions.explanation: Continuous means without gaps. Individual, distinguishable elements characterize the discrete instead.

questions.prompt: The objects in a ___ set can be numbered using natural numbers.
questions.explanation: Countability is characterized precisely by the ability to number the objects using natural numbers. Not every infinite set is countable.

questions.prompt: Which example belongs to graph theory?

options.text: Syntax and semantics of propositional logic formulas
Properties of algebraic structures such as groups

questions.explanation: Graph theory deals with vertices, edges, and weighted graphs. The other options belong to logic, algebra, and combinatorics, respectively.

questions.prompt: An overview assigns applications as follows: **Graph theory** – data structures, route planning, and social networks. **Algebra** – cryptography and error-correcting codes. Which areas are explicitly classified in this overview as applications of graph theory? Select all correct answers.
questions.explanation: The overview lists data structures, social networks, and route planning as applications of graph theory. Cryptography is assigned to algebra.

questions.prompt: What is a proposition?

options.text: A definition without a truth value
The content of a declarative sentence

questions.explanation: A proposition is the content of a declarative sentence. The other options do not describe a proposition in the stated sense.

questions.prompt: The sentence “I saw a man on the hill with a telescope” is unambiguous because it is clear who had the telescope.
questions.explanation: The sentence is ambiguous: it is unclear whether the man or the observer had the telescope. Parentheses and punctuation can make such structures more unambiguous.

questions.prompt: Which notation stands for the quantifier “for all”?
questions.explanation: $\forall$ means “for all.” $\exists$ and $\nexists$ stand for “there exists” and “there exists no,” respectively; $\oplus$ is a logical connective.

questions.prompt: What is the logical role of the word “not”?

options.text: It is a unary logical connective.
It denotes a proposition without a truth value.
It is a quantifier over all objects.
It always combines exactly two propositions.

questions.explanation: “Not,” or $\neg$, is unary and does not combine two propositions. The other options confuse a logical connective, a quantifier, and a proposition.

questions.prompt: Which representation can also illustrate propositional forms?
questions.explanation: The lecture notes name Venn diagrams as an additional way to illustrate propositional forms.

questions.prompt: Let $A=w$ and $B=f$. What is the truth value of $A\Rightarrow B$?
questions.explanation: An implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false. Therefore, here $A\Rightarrow B=f$.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from the premises in this syllogism? All Bandersnatches are Borogoves. All Borogoves are slithy.
questions.explanation: The first statement goes from Bandersnatches to Borogoves, and the second from Borogoves to slithy. Together they imply: all Bandersnatches are slithy.

questions.prompt: Which logical connectives are symmetric when $A$ and $B$ are swapped? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: And and or retain their truth values when the propositions are swapped. Implication is asymmetric, and “not” is unary.

questions.prompt: $A\Rightarrow B\equiv$ ___
questions.explanation: The implication can be written as the logically equivalent expression $\neg A\lor B$. The negation applies to the antecedent $A$.

questions.prompt: Determine the solution set for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ of $x^2=4$.
questions.explanation: Both $x=-2$ and $x=2$ satisfy $x^2=4$. Therefore, the solution set is $\{-2,2\}$.

questions.prompt: Determine the solution set for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ of $x=2\Rightarrow x^2=4$.
questions.explanation: For $x=2$, both the antecedent and consequent are true. For every other $x$, the antecedent is false or the consequent is true; therefore, the implication is true for all real $x$.

questions.prompt:
Which step in the flowchart immediately follows substituting a value?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Aussageform"] --> B["Wert einsetzen"]
    B --> C["Wahrheitswert"]
    C --> D["Lösungsmenge"]
```

options.text: Write down the solution set directly

questions.explanation: After substitution, first check whether the proposition is true or false. Only then do you obtain a solution set or a counterexample.

questions.prompt: Determine the solution set for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ of $x^2=4\Rightarrow x=2$.
questions.explanation: For $x=-2$, $x^2=4$ is true, but $x=2$ is false. This is the only value that makes the implication false; all other real values satisfy it.

questions.prompt: Which expressions are logically equivalent to $A\Rightarrow B$? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation:
The lecture notes state $A\Rightarrow B\equiv
eg A\lor B\equiv B\lor
eg A$. In contrast, $
eg B\lor A$ describes the converse implication.

questions.prompt: The solution set of $x=2\lor\neg(x=2)$ is $\varnothing$.
questions.explanation: For every real value, either $x=2$ or $x\neq2$ is true. The propositional form is therefore true for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, so $L=\mathbb{R}$.

questions.prompt: Which connective is true exactly when one of the propositions $A$ and $B$ is true?
questions.explanation: $A\oplus B$ means “either $A$ or $B$” and is true exactly when their truth values differ.

questions.prompt: The formulas $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A$ have the same truth value for every assignment of $A$ and $B$.
questions.explanation: Implication is asymmetric. When $A=w$ and $B=f$, $A\Rightarrow B$ is false, while $B\Rightarrow A$ is true.

questions.prompt: Let $A=f$ and $B=w$. What is the truth value of $A\Leftrightarrow B$?
questions.explanation: “If and only if” is true only when both propositions have the same truth value. Here the values differ, so the formula is false.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the truth table for logical connectives are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: $A\lor B$ is true only when both $A$ and $B$ are true.
The four rows cover all assignments of $A$ and $B$.
$A\Rightarrow B$ is false exactly when $A=w$ and $B=f$.

questions.explanation: For two propositions, there are four possible assignments. The implication is false only for the true-false assignment; $\neg$ is unary, while $\lor$ is true even when only one proposition is true.

questions.prompt: Which formula is logically equivalent to $A\Leftrightarrow B$?
questions.explanation: An equivalence requires both directions: $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A$. Therefore, they are joined with $\land$.

questions.prompt: Which formula is logically equivalent to “Neither $A$ nor $B$”?
questions.explanation:
“Neither $A$ nor $B$” means that both statements are false. Therefore, $
eg(A\lor B)\equiv
eg A\land
eg B$.

questions.prompt: Determine the solution set for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ of $x^2=4\Leftrightarrow x=2$.
questions.explanation: For every real value except $x=-2$, both sides have the same truth value. At $x=-2$, the left-hand side is true and the right-hand side is false.

questions.prompt:
In the diagram, what does the branch from the truth value to the node “Counterexample” represent?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Aussageform"] --> B["Wert einsetzen"]
    B --> C["Wahrheitswert"]
    C --> D["Lösungsmenge"]
    C --> E["Gegenbeispiel"]
```

options.text: Every possible value must make the proposition false.
A single value can refute the general validity of a claim.
All values automatically belong to the solution set.

questions.explanation: A counterexample is a specific value that violates a general claim. You do not need to check all other values.

questions.prompt: Which statements apply to $x=-2$ in relation to $x^2=4\Rightarrow x=2$? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A counterexample also requires checking all other real values.
$x=-2$ is a counterexample to the general validity of the implication.

questions.explanation: For $x=-2$, the antecedent is true and the consequent is false. This value alone is therefore a counterexample; no other values need to be checked.

questions.prompt: For a propositional form, the truth value depends on the ___.
questions.explanation: A propositional form receives its truth value only after a value is substituted for the variable. Different values can therefore yield different truth values.

questions.prompt: Determine the solution set for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ of $x=2\land\neg(x=2)$.
questions.explanation: The conjunction requires both $x=2$ and $x\neq2$ to hold at the same time. This is impossible for every value.

questions.prompt: Because $\lor$ is symmetric, $A\Rightarrow B\equiv B\Rightarrow A$ also holds.
questions.explanation: The symmetry of $\lor$ swaps only its two operands. In $A\Rightarrow B\equiv\neg A\lor B$, the negation remains attached to $A$; reversing the implication would attach it to $B$.

questions.prompt: Determine the solution set for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ of $((x=2)\lor\neg(x=2))\land(x^2=4\Rightarrow x=2)$.
questions.explanation: The first part is true for every $x$. The solution set is therefore determined by the second implication, which is false only at $x=-2$.

questions.prompt: Let $A=f$ and $B=f$. Which statements are true? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: When both propositions are false, the implication is true because its antecedent is false. The equivalence is also true because both values are equal; XOR and AND are false.

questions.prompt: What conclusion follows from the two premises? All $X$ are $Y$. All $Y$ are $Z$.
questions.explanation: The inference form does not depend on the names of the groups: membership in $X$ leads through $Y$ to $Z$. Therefore, “All $X$ are $Z$” follows.

What does the final node in this verification process represent? ```mermaid flowchart LR A["x² = 4 ⇒ x = 2"] --> B["x = -2 einsetzen"] B --> C["Prämisse wahr
Schluss falsch"] C --> D["Gegenbeispiel"] ```

options.text: A counterexample that refutes the general validity of the implication.
The solution set of all propositional forms.
The definition of a countable set.
A proof that the implication is true for all $x$.

questions.explanation: For $x=-2$, $x^2=4$ is true, but $x=2$ is false. This refutes the general validity of the implication.

questions.prompt: $A\oplus B\equiv((___ A)\Leftrightarrow B)$
questions.explanation: The given equivalence is $A\oplus B\equiv(\neg A\Leftrightarrow B)$. The negation ensures that the two sides have different truth values.

questions.prompt: Because $\lor$ is symmetric, $\Rightarrow$ is also symmetric.
questions.explanation: Implication is explicitly asymmetric. Although its representation $\neg A\lor B$ allows reordering within the disjunction, the roles of $A$ and $B$ cannot be swapped.

questions.prompt: Which pairings of propositional forms and solution sets are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: The first three pairings match the stated solution sets. The last proposition is false for every value, so its solution set is $\varnothing$, not $\{2\}$.

questions.prompt: For $A=w$ and $B=f$, what is the truth value of “Neither $A$ nor $B$”?

options.text: The value depends on the order.
The formula is undefined for mixed values.

questions.explanation:
“Neither $A$ nor $B$” is equivalent to $
eg A\land
eg B$. Since $A=w$, $
eg A$ is false, so the entire conjunction is false.

questions.prompt: Which classification is fully correct?
questions.explanation: The lecture notes classify $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, and $\mathbb{Q}$ as countable, and $\mathbb{R}$ as uncountable.

questions.prompt: Which pairings of topics and content are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Graph theory: data structures, route planning, and social networks
Combinatorics: counting implicitly defined sets, discrete probability, and runtime analysis
Algebra: continuous modeling of space and time
Logic: syntax and semantics of propositional logic formulas

questions.explanation: The first three pairings match the stated topics and applications. Continuous modeling of space and time is not classified under algebra; it is presented as a contrast to the discrete.

questions.prompt: Two logical expressions look different. What is the most reliable way to check whether they are logically equivalent?

options.text: Construct a truth table and compare the columns

questions.explanation: When in doubt, construct a truth table. If the result columns are identical, the expressions have the same truth values.

levels.title: Practice: Logic, Filters, and Number Sense

questions.prompt: You are building an app rule: if location sharing is enabled, the app allows navigation. Which logical structure fits?
questions.explanation: The rule is an implication: enabled location sharing $S$ implies navigation access $F$. The reverse direction would be a different statement because implications are asymmetric.

questions.prompt: You are searching a university database for all events that are **(online or in Garching)** and **still have places available**. Which structure matches the search?
questions.explanation: The parentheses first group the two location options; this is then combined with the “places available” condition. This shows how logical connectives and unambiguous structuring determine search queries.

questions.prompt: You are testing a rule with five independent yes/no conditions. How many rows does the complete truth table need to include every assignment?
questions.explanation: Each of the five variables has two possible truth values. Therefore, there are $2^5=32$ assignments and exactly 32 table rows.

questions.prompt: Is this correct: a navigation system can model intersections as vertices, roads as edges, and travel times as edge weights to calculate a route.
questions.explanation: This is a weighted graph: vertices represent intersections, edges represent roads, and weights can represent travel times. Such models are used in route planning.

questions.prompt: A banking app requires both a correct device code **and** a confirmed TAN for a transfer. Which propositional form fits?
questions.explanation: Both conditions must be true at the same time, so the connective “and” applies: $C\land T$. The other connectives describe different authorization rules.

questions.prompt: A 4-digit PIN is allowed on a combination lock: digits from 0 to 9, leading zeros, and repeated digits are allowed. How many different PINs are there?
questions.explanation: There are 10 possibilities for each of the four positions. Thus, there are $10\cdot10\cdot10\cdot10=10^4=10.000$ PINs.

questions.prompt: Let $P$ be the proposition “A package is marked as delivered” and $Q$ the proposition “The shop displays a delivery confirmation.” The rule is $P \Rightarrow Q$. Here, “reversing” explicitly means taking the converse $Q \Rightarrow P$. Two propositions are logically equivalent if they have the same truth value for every possible assignment of truth values. Are $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q \Rightarrow P$ logically equivalent?
questions.explanation: No. Under the assignment $P=falsch$, $Q=wahr$, $P \Rightarrow Q$ is true, but $Q \Rightarrow P$ is false. The converse is therefore not always logically equivalent to the original implication.

questions.prompt: A set contains 8 distinguishable elements. How many different subsets are there, including the empty set and the entire set?
questions.explanation: For each of the 8 elements, you independently choose whether to include it. Therefore, the power set has $2^8=256$ subsets.

questions.prompt: You are building an Excel filter for entries that are neither blocked nor archived. Let $G$ = “blocked” and $A$ = “archived.” Which two formulas describe the same condition?
questions.explanation:
By De Morgan's law, $
eg(G\lor A)\equiv
eg G\land
eg A$. Both filters pass exactly the rows that are neither blocked nor archived.

questions.prompt: In Sudoku, you check possible numbers for an empty cell. Each number $x$ is substituted into the rules, leaving exactly the permitted candidates. Which concept does this illustrate?

options.text: The solution set of a propositional form
An expression in the Dyck language
An implication whose direction does not matter
A truth table for two independent propositions

questions.explanation: The Sudoku rules form a propositional form with the variable $x$. The solution set contains all substituted values for which the conditions are true.
